result.markdown: --- title: "Exponential (λ = 1)" subtitle: "A strongly right-skewed population: think waiting times" --- ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="Show the simulation code"} source("../R/clt_functions.R") rgen <- function(n) rexp(n, rate = 1) # one sample of size n mu <- 1 # population mean sigma <- 1 # population SD pop_skew <- 2 # population skewness pop_kurt <- 6 # population excess kurtosis # Stage 1: a coarse grid of sample sizes. Stage 2 (automatic): every n # between the last coarse n that failed and the first one that passed. coarse <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 45, 60, 80, 100, 150, 200, 300, 400, 450, 500, 600, 750, 1000) exper <- run_with_refinement(rgen, coarse, mu, sigma) res <- exper$results n_main <- smallest_normal_n(res) n_std <- n_by_standard(res) at <- function(k) res[res$n == k, ] n_first <- min(res$n[res$normal_enough]) # first n that passes at all save_results(res, "exponential") save_summary(res, "Exponential(1)", n_main, prediction = "45", key_note = "Skewness is the bottleneck; theory predicts (2/0.25)^2 = 64") ``` ::: ::: {.answer-box} n = 71 under my main standard (strict standard: ≈ 600 · lenient standard: ≈ 20 · my prediction: 45) ::: ## 1. What population am I sampling from? The exponential distribution describes waiting times: the time until the next customer arrives, the next call comes in, or a machine fails. Most waits are short, but occasionally a wait is very long, which gives the distribution a long right tail. | Property | Value | |---|---| | Mean μ | 1 | | Standard deviation σ | 1 | | Skewness | 2 (strong right skew) | | Excess kurtosis | 6 (heavy right tail) | | Theoretical SE of the mean | σ/√n = 1/√n | ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(student_id) style_par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1)) x <- rexp(100000, rate = 1) hist(x[x < 8], breaks = 60, freq = FALSE, col = adjustcolor(pal$bars, 0.75), border = "white", main = "", xlab = "Waiting time", ylab = "Density") curve(dexp(x, 1), add = TRUE, col = pal$curve, lwd = 2.2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The population itself: 100,000 draws from Exponential(1) with the true density.](03_exponential_files/figure-html/fig-population-1.png){#fig-population width=990} ::: ::: ## 2. What did I expect before running the simulation? > I based my prediction on a pilot run at n = 1, 15 and 20. The skewness of the sample means dropped > from 0.52 at n = 15 to 0.45 at n = 20, and I extrapolated that it would reach my 0.25 limit around > **n = 45**. From the river-length example (see [Real data](06_real_world_data.qmd)) I already > expected that n = 30 would not be enough for a strongly skewed population. ## 3. Which sample sizes did I investigate? I used the same two-stage search for every population: 1. **Coarse grid:** n = 1, 2, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 45, 60, 80, 100, 150, 200, 300, 400, 450, 500, 600, 750, 1000, wide enough to cover both the main and the strict standard. 2. **Refinement:** every n from 61 to 79, the gap between the last coarse n that failed and the first one that passed. For every n I simulated **B = 100,000** sample means with seed 9426. B only controls how precisely each sample size is measured; it is not the sample size. ## 4. Results ### The four checks as n grows ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_convergence(res, chosen_n = n_main, theory_skew = pop_skew, theory_kurt = pop_kurt) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The four numerical checks. Shaded band = pass zone; green = pass, red = fail. Orange curves are the theoretical values 2/√n and 6/n; the dotted line is the chosen n.](03_exponential_files/figure-html/fig-convergence-1.png){#fig-convergence width=990} ::: ::: Skewness is clearly the bottleneck here. Excess kurtosis passes already at n = 15, but the skewness falls slowly, following the theoretical curve 2/√n almost exactly. The Q-Q correlation and the tail check cross their limits at about the same point as the skewness, which is what my calibration in [Method](../methods.qmd) was designed to do. ### Histograms of the sample means ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} n_show <- c(1, 5, 30, 45, n_main, 300) plot_hist_grid(exper, n_show, mu, sigma) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Sampling distribution of the mean (bars) and the normal curve predicted by the CLT (red).](03_exponential_files/figure-html/fig-hist-1.png){#fig-hist width=990} ::: ::: ### Normal Q-Q plots ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_qq_grid(exper, n_show) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Normal Q-Q plots. The upward bend at the right end is the leftover right skew.](03_exponential_files/figure-html/fig-qq-1.png){#fig-qq width=990} ::: ::: ### Simulation vs. theory ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_se_check(res) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The SD of the simulated means (dots) follows σ/√n (line) at every n.](03_exponential_files/figure-html/fig-se-1.png){#fig-se width=990} ::: ::: Across all 39 sample sizes, the simulated mean stayed within 0.0012 of μ = 1, and the ratio of simulated SE to σ/√n stayed between 0.998 and 1.007. The formula for the standard error holds at every n, even at n = 1 where the shape is far from normal. **The SE is right long before the shape is.** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Full results When did the sampling distribution become approximately normal? $$\boxed{n = 71}$$ ::: {#tbl-standards .cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} |Standard | Max |skewness|| Smallest n| |:----------------------|------------------------:|----------:| |Strict | 0.10| 600| |**Main (my standard)** | 0.25| **71**| |Lenient | 0.50| 20| ::: ::: ## 6. Why did I choose that value? - At **n = 71** all four checks pass: skewness 0.243, excess kurtosis 0.104, Q-Q correlation 0.9984, and tails of 1.83% / 3.13%. **Every larger n I tested also passes.** - n = 69 already passes, but n = 70 fails again, so I do not stop there. Near the threshold the skewness is sitting right at 0.25, and at B = 100,000 it is only measured to about ±0.008. My rule of taking the first n after which *every* tested n passes keeps one lucky simulation from deciding the answer. - Theory agrees: the skewness of the mean is 2/√n, which equals 0.25 at n = (2/0.25)² = **64**. - **n = 30 is not enough.** At n = 30 the skewness is still 0.36, and a "95%" interval misses 3.4% of the time on the high side but only 1.4% on the low side. ## 7. What surprised me? > My prediction of 45 was too low; the final answer was 71. At n = 45 the histogram already > looked normal to me, but the numbers did not agree. The skewness was still 0.30, > and only 1.6% of the means fell below the lower 1.96 SE limit instead of 2.5%. > I saw the same pattern with the river lengths at n = 30: the histogram looked fine, but the Q-Q plot > still curved. I learned not to rely on the histogram alone. ## 8. Reproducibility experiment: a different seed The assignment asks to rerun one analysis with a different seed. I reran the full two-stage search with seed **2026** instead of 9426. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} exper2 <- run_with_refinement(rgen, coarse, mu, sigma, seed = 2026) res2 <- exper2$results n_main2 <- smallest_normal_n(res2) cmp <- data.frame( Seed = c(student_id, 2026), `Chosen n (main)` = c(n_main, n_main2), `Strict n` = c(n_std[["strict"]], n_by_standard(res2)[["strict"]]), `Lenient n` = c(n_std[["lenient"]], n_by_standard(res2)[["lenient"]]), `Skewness at n = 30` = f3(c(at(30)$skewness, res2$skewness[res2$n == 30])), `Skewness at n = 100` = f3(c(at(100)$skewness, res2$skewness[res2$n == 100])), check.names = FALSE) write.csv(cmp, "../results/reproducibility.csv", row.names = FALSE) knitr::kable(cmp, align = "r") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | Seed| Chosen n (main)| Strict n| Lenient n| Skewness at n = 30| Skewness at n = 100| |----:|---------------:|--------:|---------:|------------------:|-------------------:| | 9426| 71| 600| 20| 0.360| 0.198| | 2026| 69| 600| 20| 0.378| 0.189| ::: ::: **Did the exact results change?** Yes. Every number in the table moved slightly, because a different seed produces different random samples. **Did my scientific conclusion change?** No. Both seeds put the threshold in the same narrow range around the theoretical value of 64, both show that n = 30 is not enough, and both show skewness as the bottleneck. With B = 100,000 the Monte Carlo noise is small compared with the effects I am measuring. A seed makes a result **reproducible** (anyone can get exactly my numbers); a large B makes it **reliable** (the conclusion does not depend on the seed).
